title: Breakthroughs and Blind Alleys: The Human Reality of Scientific Discovery
paragraphs: Popular accounts of scientific discovery tend to present it as a heroic narrative: a lone genius has a flash of insight, conducts a decisive experiment, and changes the world. This narrative is not entirely false — individual insight does matter — but it is significantly incomplete. The reality of scientific discovery is more collaborative, more incremental, and more contingent on circumstance than the heroic narrative suggests. Understanding this reality does not diminish the achievement of science; it makes it more impressive, not less.

Most scientific advances build on prior work in ways that are not always visible in the final published result. Isaac Newton famously wrote that he had stood "on the shoulders of giants" — acknowledging that his law of universal gravitation depended on the astronomical observations of Tycho Brahe, the planetary laws of Johannes Kepler, and the mathematical tools being developed by contemporaries like Leibniz. The breakthrough was Newton's, but the scaffold on which it was built was the work of many others. This is typical of science: the decisive moment of synthesis is usually preceded by decades of preparatory work by many researchers.

Chance and serendipity play a larger role in scientific discovery than the heroic narrative admits. Alexander Fleming discovered penicillin when he noticed that a mould had contaminated a Petri dish and was killing the surrounding bacteria — a discovery that would not have happened if he had not left the dish unattended, or if the mould had not blown in from a mycology laboratory two floors below. Wilhelm Röntgen discovered X-rays while experimenting with cathode ray tubes. Henri Becquerel discovered radioactivity by accidentally leaving uranium salts on top of a photographic plate. In each case, the scientist was prepared to recognise the significance of an unexpected result — but the discovery depended heavily on circumstance.

The process of science also involves a great deal of failure. For every successful experiment there are typically many more that produce null results — no effect, no difference, no confirmation of the hypothesis. These null results are scientifically important, but they are rarely published, because journals have historically preferred to publish positive findings. This "publication bias" means that the published scientific literature overrepresents positive results and underrepresents null results, which can make the evidence base for a particular finding look much stronger than it actually is.

Science is also not the purely rational enterprise it sometimes appears to be. Kuhn's influential concept of "paradigm shifts" — described in his 1962 book The Structure of Scientific Revolutions — suggests that science advances not only through the gradual accumulation of evidence but also through occasional revolutionary moments in which an entire framework of understanding is overthrown and replaced. The transition from a geocentric to a heliocentric model of the solar system, or from Newtonian to relativistic physics, required not just new evidence but a wholesale change in how scientists thought about the fundamental nature of the phenomenon being studied.

The sociology of science — how scientific communities function, how ideas gain acceptance, and how resources are distributed — has an enormous influence on which questions get studied and which findings get believed. Scientists who challenge established paradigms often face significant resistance, regardless of the quality of their evidence. Ignaz Semmelweis, who correctly identified hand-washing as a means of preventing childbed fever in the 1840s, was dismissed and institutionalised by a medical establishment unwilling to accept findings that implied their own practices were responsible for patient deaths.

None of this should lead to the conclusion that science is simply a social construction or that its findings are no more reliable than any other form of knowledge. The self-correcting mechanisms of science — peer review, replication, open data — do eventually produce reliable knowledge, even if the process is slower, messier, and more human than the heroic narrative suggests. The history of science is not a story of smooth progress, but it is a story of progressive convergence on truth — a convergence that has produced vaccines, antibiotics, semiconductors, and a working model of the universe that is astonishing in its explanatory power.

task1Items.correct: Revolutionary moments when an entire scientific framework is overthrown and replaced — not just gradual accumulation

task1Items.correct: He was dismissed and institutionalised despite correctly identifying hand-washing as a means to prevent childbed fever
